792.title: Subha and the stranger
792.hook: a man blocks Subha's path in a mango grove, praising her eyes; she shows him what an eye is (Therigatha, Subha)
792.howItsDone: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist practice for loosening desire, and teachers sometimes tell Subha's story to show that practice used as a clear refusal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambapali walked through her own body, then and now. Your line was so it was, so it is. Did you meet your reflection without a verdict? Today, another nun, and a man who won't let her pass. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

A path through a mango grove, the one known as Jivaka's. A nun named Subha is walking it. A man steps into her way and stays there. What wrong have I done you, she asks, that you stand in my path? It isn't fitting for a man to touch a woman who has gone forth. He doesn't step aside. He starts talking instead: about her youth, about the forest in flower, and more than anything, about her eyes. What she says back is today's lesson.
screen: `JIVAKA'S MANGO GROVE.` → `A MAN BLOCKS THE PATH.` → `WHAT WRONG HAVE I DONE YOU?`

segments.voice: First, his pitch. In the poem he offers her a life of comfort: fine cloth, ornaments, a house, the grove in bloom and full of birdsong. Give up the robe, he says. And he keeps returning to her eyes, like a doe's, he says; nothing is dearer to him. Second, her answer. Subha takes his praise apart. What is this body you're so taken with? What is an eye? A little ball set in a hollow, she says, with a bubble in the middle and tears around it. She compares a body to a painted puppet. She has seen through what he's selling. Third, the act. Then the poem does something startling. She plucks out her eye and holds it out to him: here, take it. His desire vanishes on the spot. He asks her forgiveness, and wishes her well, and lets her go. Fourth, the ending. Subha goes on to the Buddha, and the poem says that when she saw him, her eye was restored as it had been. What to make of a story like this? Some readers hear renunciation pushed to its limit. Others hear a woman refusing to be reduced to a part of her body: he wanted the eye, so she showed him what an eye is. The poem tells it as her answer, once, not as a thing anyone is asked to repeat. And its first line still stands on its own: she names the wrong plainly, before anything else happens.
screen: `A HOUSE, CLOTH, AND HER EYES.` · `A BALL IN A HOLLOW, WITH TEARS.` · `HERE, TAKE YOUR EYE.` · `SEEING THE BUDDHA, MADE WHOLE.` · then, large: `WHAT IS AN EYE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refuse one unwanted advance. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It might be a sales pitch, a pull from your phone, a request you keep saying yes to out of habit. Settle, and bring it to mind. Then hear Subha's first question inside: what wrong have I done, that you stand in my path? Let a no form, plain and unhurried. You don't have to say it yet. Just feel what it's like to hold it. And if someone is truly blocking your path the way the man in the grove did, that calls for more than a breath: tell someone you trust. The bell holds the time.
Subha and the stranger. A nun stopped on a forest path and praised for her eyes, who answered with a question: what is an eye? Today's word.
Your line: what is an eye. Today, when something is praised to sell it to you, ask Subha's question of it: what is this, really? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

793.title: Punnika's question
793.hook: a water-carrier asks a brahmin: if bathing washed away evil, wouldn't the fish and frogs be saints? (Therigatha, Punnika)
793.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers read Punnika's verses as a teaching that purity comes from conduct and intention, and tell of a water-carrier whose plain question changed a priest's life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subha answered a stranger in the grove. Your line was what is an eye. Did you ask what something really was, while it was being sold to you? Today, another woman with a question, at a river. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

Why would anyone stand in a river in the cold if they didn't have to? Punnika has to. She carries water for a household, and in her verses she says she goes down into the water in the cold, afraid of her mistresses' punishment. At the river she finds a brahmin, a priest, standing in the water, shivering. She's there because she has to be. Why is he? So she asks him. Her question, his answer, and hers: that's today.
screen: `A WATER-CARRIER IN THE COLD.` → `A BRAHMIN, SHIVERING.` → `WHY ARE YOU HERE?`

segments.voice: First, her question. Brahmin, what are you afraid of, she asks, that you go down into the water with your limbs shaking in the cold? She knows what drives her. She wonders what drives him. Second, his answer. He's doing good to undo evil, he says. Whoever has done wrong, young or old, is freed of it by bathing. Third, the frogs. Who told you that, she asks, someone who didn't know, telling someone else who didn't? If water washed away wrongdoing, then the frogs and the turtles, the water snakes and the crocodiles would all go to heaven. Then she presses further. If the river carried off your wrongs, it would carry off your good deeds too, and leave you with nothing. Fourth, what she offers instead. If you fear suffering, she says, don't do harmful things, openly or in secret. And she adds a kindness: don't let your body suffer in the cold. The brahmin is moved. In the poem he thanks her for turning him from the wrong road and takes refuge, and the poem ends with him saying that now he is truly washed. The washing still matters. It has moved from the skin to the deeds. This poem is one voice in an old conversation, told from inside the Buddha's community; in the Majjhima the Buddha makes a similar point about bathing in sacred rivers. Hindus who bathe in holy rivers today speak for themselves about what that bathing means, and this poem doesn't speak for them.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU AFRAID OF?` · `WATER WASHES OFF WRONGDOING.` · `THEN THE FROGS GO TO HEAVEN.` · `FROM THE SKIN TO THE DEEDS.` · then, large: `THE FROGS WOULD BE SAINTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one ritual, gently. Choose one thing you do by habit, small or large: a way you start the morning, a phrase you always say, a custom from your family or your faith. Settle, and hold it in mind. Then ask it Punnika's question, the way she asked, plainly: what is this for? You don't need to stop doing it. Sometimes the answer makes it richer. Just ask, and listen for what comes back. The bell holds the time.
Punnika's question. A water-carrier asks a shivering brahmin why he bathes, and turns him from the river to the deeds themselves. Today's word.
Your line: the frogs would be saints. Today, catch one thing you do out of habit, and ask, kindly, what it's really for. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

what it means: a water-carrier asks why a brahmin bathes in the cold to wash off wrongdoing, and turns him from the river to his deeds.

794.title: Isidasi's story
794.hook: three husbands sent her back; she tells the long tale behind it (Therigatha, Isidasi)
794.howItsDone: Isidasi's poem is read in Buddhist communities as a teaching on kamma across lives, and modern readers also discuss it as an account of a woman's marriages told in her own voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punnika asked a shivering brahmin why he bathed. Your line was the frogs would be saints. Did you ask, kindly, what one habit was really for? Today, a nun who is asked why, and answers at length. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

Two nuns sit together after the alms round, in the city of Pataliputta. One of them, Bodhi, asks the other a question that's half compliment and half puzzle. You're still young, and lovely, she says. What did you see that made you leave the world? The other nun is Isidasi. She doesn't answer with a slogan. She tells the whole story, and it's long, and it doesn't flatter anyone, not even herself. Today's lesson is a woman who was asked why, and told everything.
screen: `TWO NUNS AFTER THE ALMS ROUND.` → `WHY DID YOU LEAVE THE WORLD?` → `SHE TELLS EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: First, the faithful wife. Isidasi says she was married into a merchant family in Saketa, and she did all a daughter-in-law was expected to do. She bowed to her in-laws morning and evening, cooked, cleaned, served her husband with her own hands. And still he came to hate her. When his parents asked what she had done, she told them: nothing. I've done no wrong. They sent her home to her father. Second, again and again. Her father gave her to a second husband, who sent her back too. Then her father invited a wandering beggar to stay as his son-in-law. Before long the man asked for his begging bowl and robe back, and left. Three times, and no one could name a fault. So, with her father's blessing, she went forth. Third, the longer story. Here the poem turns. Isidasi says she can now see her past lives, and she tells them: once a goldsmith who went after other men's wives, then long suffering, then births as animals, then hard human lives. In her telling, being sent away in this life was that old deed ripening. Fourth, how to hear it. Some readers find this ending hard, because it can sound like blaming a woman for being rejected. But notice what the poem insists on first: in this life she did nothing wrong. Her husbands couldn't name a fault, and neither could she. The past-life story is her searching out the whole shape of what happened, further back than one life, and then setting it down. She ends the poem free of all of it.
screen: `A FAITHFUL WIFE, SENT HOME.` · `TWICE MORE, AND NO FAULT FOUND.` · `A GOLDSMITH, LIVES AGO.` · `BLAMELESS NOW, AND FREE AT LAST.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to listen to someone's whole story. Bring to mind a person whose life you know only by its headline: the divorce, the move, the illness, the job that ended. Settle. Picture asking them, the way Bodhi asked Isidasi, how did it happen? Then picture not interrupting. Not fixing. Letting the story be as long as it is. Breathe into that patience now, so it's ready when the moment comes. The bell holds the time.
Isidasi's story. Asked why she left the world, a nun told all of it: marriages that failed through no fault she could find, and a past that reached back through other lives. Today's word.
Your line: the whole story. Today, when someone tells you what happened, ask one more question before you decide what you think. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

what a scholar hears: the poem is framed as a dialogue, Bodhi's question and Isidasi's answer, and its past-life section traces kamma through a chain of births, ending in her freedom from it.

795.title: Sumedha refuses
795.hook: a princess refuses marriage to a king, cuts her hair and argues her way to the order (Therigatha, Sumedha)
795.howItsDone: In Buddhist traditions, going forth as a nun or monk is a decision families take seriously, and the Therigatha's stories of women who argued for it, like Sumedha's, are read as examples of resolve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isidasi told Bodhi all of it. Your line was the whole story. Did you ask one more question before deciding what you thought? Today, a princess who says no to a king. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

A sword, used for a haircut. Sumedha is a king's daughter in the city of Mantavati, and she has been promised in marriage to another king, Anikaratta. She has heard the nuns teach, and she wants to go forth. Her parents want the wedding. The poem that tells her story is long, and much of it is talk: argument after argument from a young woman who will not be talked out of what she has chosen. Today, how she wins.
screen: `A PRINCESS, PROMISED TO A KING.` → `SHE WANTS TO GO FORTH.` → `ARGUMENT AFTER ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the argument at home. Sumedha tells her parents she wants to go forth, and they weep and plead: a royal marriage is waiting for her. She answers them with the teaching. Life is short, she says, and pleasures don't last. She reaches for pictures the Buddha's discourses use for sense pleasures: a dream that ends on waking, goods that are only borrowed. She isn't sulking. She's making a case. Second, the hair. When the pleading doesn't stop, she acts. She cuts off her own hair with a sword, shuts the palace doors, and sits down. The poem says she entered the first stage of meditative absorption, right there. Third, the king. Anikaratta arrives, dressed for a wedding, with gold and jewels, and he offers her wealth and every pleasure a kingdom has. She doesn't run, and she doesn't give in. She answers him, as patiently as she argued with her parents. Fourth, the result. In the poem, the king ends up asking her father to let her go forth. She wins, not by slipping away in the night, but by making her case to every person standing in the doorway, until there is no one left to persuade. Her refusal is a no to the wedding, and a yes to something she can explain. That's the shape the poem gives her. She argued her way in.
screen: `SHE ANSWERS HER PARENTS.` · `HAIR CUT, DOORS SHUT, SHE SITS.` · `THE KING ARRIVES WITH GOLD.` · `EVEN THE KING ASKS FOR HER.` · then, large: `SHE ARGUED HER WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by one decision. Bring to mind a choice you've made that someone questions, or that you keep reopening yourself. Settle. Then say your reasons to yourself, plainly, one by one, the way Sumedha laid hers out. Notice which reasons hold when you say them. If the decision still stands, let yourself stand with it, calmly, for these breaths. If it doesn't, that's worth knowing too. The bell holds the time.
Sumedha refuses. A princess promised to a king, who cut her hair, shut the doors, and argued until even the king asked that she be let go. Today's word.
Your line: she argued her way in. Today, when a choice of yours is questioned, give one clear reason, kindly, instead of giving in or walking out. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

what a scholar hears: much of the poem is argument, and the pictures she uses for sense pleasures, a dream, borrowed goods, also appear in the Buddha's discourses, as in the Majjhima's Potaliya Sutta.

796.title: Sona's strength
796.hook: the mother of ten who ordained late: effort in old age (Therigatha, Sona)
796.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, people sometimes ordain or take up serious practice late in life, and Sona's verses are remembered as a sign that effort on the path does not depend on youth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sumedha talked a king out of a wedding. Your line was she argued her way in. Did you give one clear reason, kindly, when a choice of yours was questioned? Today, a nun who came late, and the strength she found. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

Shame on you, wretched old age. That's how Sona's song ends, and it reads almost like a dare. The path has met her before, in the commentary's story of a late start and a pot of bath water. Today stays with her own verses. She bore ten sons, she says, and by the time she went to a nun to hear the teaching, she was weak and old. No royal refusal, no dramatic escape. A tired body and a decision. Today, the strength she found late.
screen: `SHAME ON YOU, OLD AGE.` → `TODAY, HER OWN VERSES.` → `WEAK AND OLD, SHE GOES.`

segments.voice: First, where she started. Having borne ten sons from this body, she says, weak and old, I went to a nun. She doesn't dress it up. Her strength was gone before her practice began. Second, what she heard. The nun taught her the basics: the heaps that make up a person, the senses, the elements. Sona heard it, cut off her hair, and went forth. Nothing in her verses says she waited to feel stronger first. Third, what she found. Her verses move quickly now. While she trained, she says, the divine eye was made clear, and she came to know her former lives. Her mind became steady and one-pointed. She was freed, clinging to nothing, at peace. The heaps that make up a person, she says, are fully known, and stand now cut off at the root. Fourth, the dare. Then she turns to old age itself. Shame on you, she says, wretched old age; there's no more coming back. Old age had taken her strength of body. It hadn't taken her effort. The strength in the title isn't muscle. In Sona's song it's the will to keep at it, and it didn't wait for her to be young.
screen: `TEN SONS, THEN WEAK AND OLD.` · `SHE HEARS, CUTS HER HAIR, GOES.` · `A STEADY MIND, AND FREED.` · `SHAME ON YOU, OLD AGE.` · then, large: `STRENGTH IN OLD AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one hard thing to do today, sized to the body you have now. A walk you've been putting off. A phone call. A chore that keeps waiting. Settle first, and let the breath be easy. Picture the hard thing clearly: where you'll be, what the first step is. Notice any voice that says too tired, too old, too late. Don't argue with it. Just let Sona sit beside it, the nun who started weak and old. Then pick a time. The bell holds the time.
Sona's strength. The mother of ten sons who went forth weak and old, was freed, and told old age it had lost. Today's word.
Your line: strength in old age. Today, do the one hard thing you chose, at whatever pace your body allows. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

797.title: The brothers' songs
797.hook: poems of the first monks: forests, rain, freedom
797.howItsDone: In Theravada communities, verses from the Theragatha are read and taught alongside the Therigatha, and teachers often draw on single poems from it as short reflections.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona, who came to the order late and found her strength there. Your line was strength in old age. Did you do one hard thing? Today, the songs turn from the sisters to the brothers. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

Rain on a thatched roof. A peacock calling somewhere in the trees. A man sitting alone in a forest, saying out loud that he is free. These aren't scenes from a novel. They're lines from poems that Buddhist tradition gives to the early monks themselves. Lately we've been listening to the sisters' songs, the Therigatha. It has a companion, a book of the brothers' songs, and today we open it. Today's word is its name.
screen: `RAIN ON A THATCHED ROOF.` → `THE SISTERS' BOOK HAS A COMPANION.` → `TODAY WE OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Theragatha. A thera is an elder, a senior monk, and a gatha is a verse. Verses of the elders. Second, the voice. Each poem carries a monk's name, and tradition says the monk himself spoke it, often about the moment he was freed, or looking back on the road there. So these aren't sermons about the monks. They're his own words, in the first person: I went to the forest, I sat, I was set free. Third, what they sing about. Forests. Caves and rocky hills. Clouds and rain. Animals: peacocks, elephants, cranes. And again and again, freedom: the work is done, the burden is down, there is nothing more to do. Some poems are a single verse. Some run on for pages, and in one of them a monk argues with his own mind. Fourth, how to read them. Some readers find them strangely close to us: a man in a hut, listening to the rain, and glad. Others notice how much they repeat: the same phrases close poem after poem, almost like a chorus. Both are there: a shared chorus, and one person's afternoon of rain and peacocks. The brothers' book sits beside the sisters' book among the short texts of the Pali canon. Over the coming days we'll meet some of these brothers by name: a monk with a dry roof, a man who swept away old flowers, a former bandit, an actor, the great disciples. Each one, in his own words.
screen: `THERA, AN ELDER. GATHA, A VERSE.` · `EACH POEM CARRIES A MONK'S NAME.` · `FORESTS, RAIN AND FREEDOM.` · `A CHORUS, AND ONE MAN'S AFTERNOON.` · then, large: `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one short poem. Any poem will do, from an old book or a new one, or one you've known by heart since school. Read it slowly, once, out loud if you can. Then put it down and sit. Let one line stay with you. Not its meaning, just its sound, or its picture: rain, a hill, a bird. When the mind wanders off, come back to that one line, the way you'd come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Theragatha. The verses of the elders: songs the tradition gives to the early monks, spoken in their own voices. Today's word.
Your line: his own words. Today, when someone tells you something in their own words, not a report about it, listen a little longer than usual. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

original.note: Pali: thera, an elder, and gatha, a verse. The verses of the elders.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rulebook for monks.
what it means: a book of poems, each given to an early monk, about forests, rain, and being set free.
what a scholar hears: thera, elder; gatha, verse. the brothers' book sits beside the sisters' Therigatha among the short texts of the Pali canon.

798.title: My hut is roofed
798.hook: Subhuti: my hut is roofed and snug; rain, god, if you like (Theragatha 1.1)
798.howItsDone: Forest monks in the Theravada tradition still live in small huts called kutis, and teachers often read Subhuti's short poem as a picture of a mind at ease whatever the weather.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Theragatha, the brothers' songs. Your line was his own words. Did you listen a little longer to someone? Today, the poem that stands at the head of that book. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

A roof, a mind, and a dare to the weather. A monk named Subhuti sits in a small hut, and what he says to the sky is the poem numbered first in the brothers' book. It isn't a plea for the rain to stop. It isn't a complaint about the leaks. It's closer to an invitation. Today we read his few lines, and hear what freedom sounds like when it talks back to the weather.
screen: `A ROOF, A MIND, A DARE.` → `A MONK IN A SMALL HUT.` → `HE TALKS BACK TO THE SKY.`

segments.voice: First, the hut. Subhuti says his hut is roofed, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind. A small thing, done well. In the wet season, a good roof is the difference between sitting through the night and running for cover. Second, the mind. In the same breath he says his mind is well settled, and freed. The hut and the mind sit side by side in the poem, two shelters, both finished. One keeps the water out. The other no longer lets the old storms in. Third, the dare. So rain, god, if you like, he says. The poem speaks to the rain as a god, the one who sends it. And Subhuti isn't asking that god for anything. Rain, or don't. He's covered either way. Fourth, why it's a fitting door into the book. The poem is tiny. But it holds the whole Theragatha in small: the forest, the weather, a man alone, and the quiet news that the work is done. Some readers hear a little swagger in it. Others hear relief, the voice of someone who used to dread the storm and doesn't anymore. The poem doesn't say which, and it doesn't need to. A dry roof isn't nothing. Neither is a settled mind. Put the two together and the sky can do what it likes.

If not, find your shelter anyway: a chair that holds your back, a blanket on your knees, the walls around you. Notice what's covering you right now. Then turn to the mind. Is anything leaking in? A worry, a plan, a noise from the next room? Let it drip. You don't have to fix the roof today. Just sit under it. If you like, say Subhuti's words quietly to whatever's coming: rain, if you like.
